examples.knowledge_point: Parametrizing Part of a Vertical Hyperbola
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093765/assets/2944e095d71b64fb2f9e6e0121a09fb9eb2f3ffe765f9881162c95fe6875a831.png)

The quarter-hyperbola above is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x = \sqrt3\tan{t}, \qquad y = \sqrt2\sec{t}.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $t?$
examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x= \sqrt3 \tan{t}, \quad
y = \sqrt2 \sec{t}, \quad
t \in [-\pi,\pi], \quad
t \neq \pm\dfrac{\pi}2.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-hyperbola, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093765/assets/b1d78a939f85c533bcd9b4609346f2a15385aad3a6b074a62b791551cf784418.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right]$ we get the required quarter-hyperbola.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe the required quarter-hyperbola are

$$
x= \sqrt3\tan{t}, \quad
y = \sqrt2\sec{t}, \quad
t \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}2,0\right].
$$

feedback.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=5\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sec}⁡t.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent Identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+1 & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
